Dynamic panel spatial probit

Source: vignettes/dynamics.Rmd
dynamics.Rmd

Outcomes observed over time are usually persistent: a region in recession this year is likely to be in recession next year, a firm that exported last year is likely to export again. Three different mechanisms produce this pattern, and they have different implications:

  • state dependence: the outcome itself changes the next period’s probability (exporting builds contacts that make the next export cheaper);
  • heterogeneity: some units are persistently more likely to have the outcome, for reasons the regressors do not capture (the random effects αi\alpha_i);
  • persistent shocks: the unobserved latent factors are themselves autocorrelated, so the propensity persists even when the outcome does not feed back.

In a spatial panel these mix with a fourth: neighbours’ outcomes. This vignette shows how panelspatialprobit separates them and how to read the dynamic effects.

library(panelspatialprobit)
W <- psp_weights(rook_weights(7, 7), style = "W")
ctrl <- psp_control(iter = 3000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, seed = 1, progress = FALSE)

State dependence: lagged outcomes

dynamic = psp_dynamic() adds the previous period’s outcome to the model:

zit=ρ(Wzt)i+γyi,t−1+η(Wyt−1)i+xit′β+αi+εit,z_{it} = \rho (Wz_t)_i + \gamma y_{i,t-1} + \eta (Wy_{t-1})_i + x_{it}'\beta + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it},

with γ\gamma reported as lag_y and, with lag_Wy = TRUE, η\eta reported as W_lag_y (the neighbours’ previous outcomes, a lagged spatial diffusion channel). For ordered outcomes the lag enters as one indicator per category above the first.

The first period has no previous outcome. It serves as the initial condition and is not modelled itself, so a panel of TT periods gives T−1T - 1 modelled periods.

The initial conditions problem

The random effect αi\alpha_i influenced the first outcome yi1y_{i1} too, so the lagged outcome is correlated with αi\alpha_i. Treating yi1y_{i1} as fixed and independent of αi\alpha_i attributes part of the heterogeneity to state dependence and overstates γ\gamma. The default, psp_dynamic(initial = "wooldridge"), follows Wooldridge (2005): it models αi\alpha_i given the initial outcome and the regressors, αi=ξ0yi1+x‾i′ξ+ai,\alpha_i = \xi_0 y_{i1} + \bar x_i'\xi + a_i, by adding init_y and the unit means of the regressors (mean_x1, …) to the model. a_i is then the random effect, independent of the initial condition.

d <- sim_psprobit(W, T = 8, beta = c(-0.4, 1, -0.8), rho = 0.4, sigma_alpha = 0.6,
                  gamma = 0.8, seed = 3)
fit <- psprobit(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d, index = c("id", "time"), W = W,
                dynamic = psp_dynamic(), impacts = FALSE, control = ctrl)
#> Warning: Possible convergence problems (R-hat > 1.01 or bulk ESS < 200) for:
#> sigma_alpha. Consider more iterations.
round(coef(fit), 2)
#> (Intercept)          x1          x2       lag_y      init_y     mean_x1 
#>       -0.59        0.74       -0.85        0.78        0.46        0.37 
#>     mean_x2         rho sigma_alpha 
#>        0.48        0.37        0.40

The warning concerns σα\sigma_\alpha, which the Wooldridge terms leave little to explain; in an application, run longer chains until it disappears. The true γ\gamma is 0.8. A pooled model that ignores the heterogeneity puts the persistence due to αi\alpha_i into lag_y:

fit_pooled <- psprobit(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d, index = c("id", "time"), W = W,
                       effects = "pooled", dynamic = psp_dynamic(initial = "none"),
                       impacts = FALSE, control = ctrl)
round(coef(fit_pooled), 2)
#> (Intercept)          x1          x2       lag_y         rho 
#>       -0.52        0.71       -0.72        0.98        0.38

One data set proves little, but the pattern is systematic. In a Monte Carlo study with 200 replications (vignette("validation")), the Wooldridge model recovered γ=0.8\gamma = 0.8 with a bias of 0.01 and 93% coverage of 90% intervals, while the pooled model overstated it by 0.31, with 11% coverage.

The coefficients of init_y and mean_* describe the random effects, not causal effects, and they receive no impacts.

Effects over time

Because today’s outcome is in tomorrow’s model, a change in a regressor keeps acting after it ends. The impacts of psp_impacts() (and fit$impacts) describe the period of the change only, the short-run effect. psp_response_path() traces the rest. It simulates the outcome histories with and without the change, using the same random numbers in both, and averages the difference in the probabilities period by period over histories and posterior draws.

A temporary change lasts one period (here, one unit of x1x_1 in the first modelled period, for all units):

psp_response_path(fit, "x1", draws = 100, nsim = 10, seed = 1)
#> Response of P(y = 1) to a temporary shock of 1 in x1 (100 draws x 10 histories)
#> 
#> Average change over all units:
#>  horizon period   mean     sd   q2.5  q97.5
#>        0      2 0.2453 0.0405 0.1721 0.3106
#>        1      3 0.0747 0.0267 0.0348 0.1359
#>        2      4 0.0226 0.0142 0.0049 0.0675
#>        3      5 0.0079 0.0072 0.0005 0.0276
#>        4      6 0.0030 0.0036 0.0000 0.0134
#>        5      7 0.0011 0.0020 0.0000 0.0062
#>        6      8 0.0005 0.0015 0.0000 0.0035

Horizon 0 is the short-run total impact. The later horizons come only from the lagged outcome: the change made the outcome more likely in period 2, which makes it more likely in period 3, and so on, decaying at a rate set by lag_y and the curvature of the probit.

A permanent change stays in place, so its effect builds up as the outcome history adjusts. With units = only some units are changed, and the effects on the changed units and on the others (the spillover) are reported separately:

psp_response_path(fit, "x1", type = "permanent", units = c("1", "2", "3"),
                  draws = 100, nsim = 10, seed = 1)
#> Response of P(y = 1) to a permanent shock of 1 in x1 (100 draws x 10 histories)
#> 
#> Average change over all units:
#>  horizon period   mean     sd   q2.5  q97.5
#>        0      2 0.0120 0.0030 0.0061 0.0182
#>        1      3 0.0155 0.0036 0.0089 0.0233
#>        2      4 0.0153 0.0036 0.0097 0.0234
#>        3      5 0.0222 0.0048 0.0147 0.0324
#>        4      6 0.0232 0.0057 0.0132 0.0331
#>        5      7 0.0217 0.0062 0.0118 0.0353
#>        6      8 0.0146 0.0047 0.0070 0.0250
#> 
#> Average change over the shocked units:
#>  horizon period   mean     sd   q2.5  q97.5
#>        0      2 0.1572 0.0445 0.0688 0.2443
#>        1      3 0.1847 0.0364 0.1187 0.2511
#>        2      4 0.1907 0.0423 0.1211 0.2640
#>        3      5 0.2988 0.0635 0.1995 0.4144
#>        4      6 0.2946 0.0672 0.1793 0.4509
#>        5      7 0.2552 0.0702 0.1246 0.3968
#>        6      8 0.1656 0.0568 0.0678 0.2792
#> 
#> Average change over the other units:
#>  horizon period   mean     sd   q2.5  q97.5
#>        0      2 0.0025 0.0010 0.0008 0.0046
#>        1      3 0.0044 0.0020 0.0014 0.0089
#>        2      4 0.0039 0.0021 0.0010 0.0086
#>        3      5 0.0042 0.0020 0.0010 0.0078
#>        4      6 0.0055 0.0025 0.0016 0.0112
#>        5      7 0.0065 0.0032 0.0020 0.0133
#>        6      8 0.0048 0.0025 0.0013 0.0104

For the changed units the effect grows over the first periods as the outcome history adjusts. It then varies from period to period, because the slope of the probit depends on where the units’ probabilities sit, which their regressors in each period determine. The effect on the other units is small: only three units changed, and only their neighbours respond.

start = sets the period of the change, and $draws holds the posterior draws of every horizon, for derived quantities such as cumulative effects.

Persistent shocks: latent dynamics

psp_dynamic(latent = TRUE) puts the persistence in the latent outcome instead (Wang and Kockelman 2009):

zt=ρWzt+γzt−1+Xtβ+α+εt,z_t = \rho W z_t + \gamma z_{t-1} + X_t\beta + \alpha + \varepsilon_t,

with γ\gamma reported as lag_z. The outcome does not feed back; what persists is the unobserved propensity, including the part of last period’s shock that the outcome did not reveal. Every period is modelled (the first one has no lag and shares α\alpha with the others), and probabilities and impacts integrate over the latent history: the variance of the latent outcome grows with tt as the lagged shocks accumulate.

d_lat <- sim_psprobit(W, T = 6, beta = c(-0.2, 1, -0.8), rho = 0.3, sigma_alpha = 0.5,
                      gamma_z = 0.5, seed = 4)
fit_lat <- psprobit(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d_lat, index = c("id", "time"), W = W,
                    dynamic = psp_dynamic(latent = TRUE),
                    control = psp_control(iter = 8000, warmup = 2000, thin = 4,
                                          chains = 2, seed = 4, progress = FALSE))
round(coef(fit_lat), 2)
#> (Intercept)          x1          x2       lag_z         rho sigma_alpha 
#>       -0.34        1.11       -0.93        0.51        0.27        0.84

The sampler updates the latent outcomes given γ\gamma and γ\gamma given the latent outcomes, and the two are strongly dependent, so latent dynamics need longer chains than the other models (above, four times the usual length, thinned). Watch the convergence warning, and see the “Convergence” section of ?psprobit.

psp_response_path() works here too; it computes the paths exactly from the reduced form, without simulating outcome histories. Latent dynamics need time-invariant weights and cannot be combined with lagged outcomes.

Which kind of persistence?

The three mechanisms produce similar outcome patterns, so the data separate them only through the model’s structure. Some guidance:

  • If theory says the outcome itself changes the conditions for the next period (adoption of a technology, participation, a sunk entry cost), use lag_y, with random effects and the Wooldridge initial condition.
  • If the persistence is in slowly moving unobserved conditions, use latent dynamics.
  • Always include random effects: without them, both kinds of dynamics absorb the heterogeneity.

psp_ppc() reports, for each period, the share of units whose outcome repeats from the previous period. A model whose replicated persistence falls short of the observed one (posterior predictive p-values near 0) is missing a source of persistence. Here we compare the dynamic model with two static models fitted to the same periods, one with random effects and one pooled:

persistence <- function(f) {
  p <- psp_ppc(f, draws = 200, seed = 1)$persistence
  round(cbind(observed = p$observed, replicated = colMeans(p$replicated), ppp = p$ppp), 2)
}
d_est <- d[d$time > 1, ]
fit_static <- psprobit(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d_est, index = c("id", "time"), W = W,
                       impacts = FALSE, control = ctrl)
fit_static_pooled <- psprobit(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d_est, index = c("id", "time"), W = W,
                              effects = "pooled", impacts = FALSE, control = ctrl)
persistence(fit)
#>             observed replicated  ppp
#> persist t=3     0.57       0.62 0.82
#> persist t=4     0.59       0.55 0.30
#> persist t=5     0.65       0.60 0.28
#> persist t=6     0.63       0.58 0.26
#> persist t=7     0.63       0.59 0.36
#> persist t=8     0.69       0.63 0.22
persistence(fit_static)
#>             observed replicated  ppp
#> persist t=3     0.57       0.60 0.74
#> persist t=4     0.59       0.56 0.36
#> persist t=5     0.65       0.58 0.16
#> persist t=6     0.63       0.59 0.28
#> persist t=7     0.63       0.58 0.27
#> persist t=8     0.69       0.60 0.14
persistence(fit_static_pooled)
#>             observed replicated  ppp
#> persist t=3     0.57       0.52 0.24
#> persist t=4     0.59       0.52 0.19
#> persist t=5     0.65       0.53 0.07
#> persist t=6     0.63       0.50 0.04
#> persist t=7     0.63       0.50 0.04
#> persist t=8     0.69       0.52 0.01

The pooled static model has no source of persistence and falls short in most periods. The static random-effects model reproduces the persistence about as well as the dynamic model, through the random effects. This is the point made at the start: the outcome patterns of state dependence and heterogeneity are similar, and a check like this one cannot choose between them. The choice rests on the substantive question and on handling the initial condition properly.

Restrictions

  • Dynamic models need a balanced panel with complete outcomes (missing outcomes would make the lagged regressors missing).
  • predict(newdata = ) is not available with lagged outcomes, because new regressors would change the outcome history. Use psp_response_path().
  • The impacts of psp_impacts() are short-run for lagged outcomes. For latent dynamics they are the effects of a change in one period on that period’s probabilities, integrating over the latent history.

References

Wang, X. and Kockelman, K. M. (2009). Bayesian inference for ordered response data with a dynamic spatial-ordered probit model. Journal of Regional Science 49, 877–913.

Wooldridge, J. M. (2005). Simple solutions to the initial conditions problem in dynamic, nonlinear panel data models with unobserved heterogeneity. Journal of Applied Econometrics 20, 39–54.
